conventions.convention: The finite dual consists of functionals annihilating a finite-codimensional two-sided ideal of a unital associative algebra. Transposed multiplication is initially only a candidate coproduct.

Coideals include the counit condition. Hopf ideals additionally are two-sided ideals stable under the antipode. Subbialgebras carry structure maps making inclusion a bialgebra map; a Hopf subalgebra must also be antipode-stable.
The quotient and tensor-product Hopf constructions are choice-free. AC is assumed only for the kernel assertion, through arbitrary-vector-space tensor-injection and tensor-kernel exactness.
Dual multiplication is convolution in the original tensor-factor order; dual coproduct evaluates as Δ(φ)(a⊗b)=φ(ab), and the dual antipode is φ↦φ∘S. No bijectivity of S is assumed.
The Taft convention is gx=ζxg, Δ(x)=1⊗x+x⊗g, and S(x)=−xg⁻¹, with basis gⁱxʲ for 0≤i,j<N, N>1, ζ primitive of order N, and char(k) not dividing N.
The coideal comparison and Sweedler examples assume characteristic different from 2; the nonzero coefficient 2 is essential in their witnesses.

The polynomial finite-dual decomposition assumes k algebraically closed. δ(a,r) extracts the coefficient of (x−a)ʳ, rather than an unnormalized derivative; binomial coefficients are interpreted in k in every characteristic.

load_bearing.statement: For a finite-dimensional Hopf k-algebra H, its full dual H* is a Hopf algebra with convolution multiplication, unit ε, coproduct transposed from multiplication, counit φ↦φ(1), and antipode φ↦φ∘S. No bijectivity assumption on S is required.

For N>1, a primitive N-th root ζ∈k, and char(k) not dividing N, the stated truncated skew multiplication defines the presented algebra k⟨g,x⟩/(gᴺ−1,xᴺ,gx−ζxg), with basis gⁱxʲ for 0≤i,j<N and the displayed Hopf maps.

For every unital associative k-algebra A, A° is a coalgebra under transposed multiplication and evaluation at 1, and its elements are exactly finite-dimensional left-module matrix coefficients. For a bialgebra H, H° is a bialgebra under convolution; for a Hopf algebra H, precomposition with S is an antipode on H°, without finite-dimensionality or bijectivity of S.

A Hopf ideal I gives H/I a unique quotient Hopf structure and the Hopf-map factorization property. Kernels of Hopf maps are Hopf ideals under AC. Tensor products of Hopf algebras carry the displayed middle-factor-flip structure and tensor-product antipode; quotient and tensor-product constructions are choice-free.
A° consists of f∈A* for which some two-sided ideal I has dimₖ(A/I)<∞ and f(I)=0.
A Hopf ideal is a two-sided ideal satisfying ε(I)=0, S(I)⊆I, and the image-based coideal condition. A Hopf subalgebra is a subbialgebra stable under S.

Unital associative algebras, central scalar maps, and unital algebra homomorphisms.
Full algebraic duals, linear functionals, and precomposition.
Repeated root extraction in the polynomial finite-dual decomposition.
The explicit AC hypothesis for arbitrary-vector-space tensor injections and the kernel branch.
Two-sided ideal closure in Hopf ideals, quotient constructions, and finite-dual annihilators.
Algebraic tensors over k, finite tensor sums, tensor units, and parenthesization conventions.
Canonical reassociation, flips, and naturality in structural-map calculations.
Finite-dimensional linear algebra, including its cited finite-subspace fact used for intersections of cofinite ideals.
Finite-dimensional tensor-dual identification with the evaluation pairing in the original factor order.
The free algebra, presented quotients, and descent of the Taft generator assignments.
AC-qualified tensor-subspace shorthand and the tensor-kernel formula in the Hopf-map kernel proof.
Polynomial monomial bases and polynomial/Laurent constructions used by the examples and their Hopf suppliers.
Tensor maps induced by linear maps and preservation of composition.
Componentwise multiplication and the unit on tensor-product algebras.
Factorization of algebra maps through quotients by killed two-sided ideals.
Nonzero tensor witnesses and comparison of coproduct coefficients in the examples.
Finite local quotient bases, principal ideal identification, and root factorization.
Decomposition of polynomial quotients into finitely many local factors and independence of their coefficient functionals.

concerns.concern: Proof 1.2 defines f=\bar f q with \bar f on A/I, but then writes “\bar f(ab)=\sum_i\bar f_i(a+I)\bar g_i(b+I)”. With a,b∈A, the left side should be f(ab), or explicitly \bar f((a+I)(b+I)). The following pullback formula uses the intended correctly typed identity.

seams_checked.note: Checked the supplier definitions and counit/Sweedler lemma against their uses. Coideals retain ε(I)=0 and image-based tensor conditions; Sweedler expressions remain finite linear contractions. No fundamental-coalgebra theorem is invoked to replace the local finite-dual proof.

Finite Hopf duality uses algebra-to-coalgebra duality only for finite-dimensional H and the stated evaluation pairing. The arbitrary finite-dual construction separately proves algebraic-tensor landing and does not infer full-dual coalgebra structure in infinite dimension.

Checked convolution, both antipode equations, uniqueness, anti-multiplication, and group/polynomial Hopf constructions against their uses. Neither dual construction assumes antipode bijectivity. The Taft proof verifies its own presentation and structural maps.

The A-page prerequisite is contextual; its companion's ex-hh-taft-module-dual uses the Taft supplier directly. The example preserves N>1, primitive ζ, the characteristic restriction, gx=ζxg, Δ(x)=1⊗x+x⊗g, and S(x)=−xg⁻¹.

The integral definition, regular-dual Hopf-module lemma, and finite-integral theorem use the full dual only in finite dimension, with convolution, counit f↦f(1), and transposed antipode exactly as supplied. Bijectivity is subsequently proved rather than imported from the dual-Hopf theorem.

The finite-double definition and coalgebra/antipode lemma cite the ordinary dual Hopf structure faithfully. They introduce opposite multiplication explicitly, retain the ordinary dual coproduct, and obtain the inverse antipode only under separately stated and supplied bijectivity.
